title: Nested Classes and Namespaces
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of nested classes and namespaces in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply nested classes and namespaces in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to organizing related types and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Nested Classes and Namespaces through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding nested classes and namespaces helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Nested Classes and Namespaces helps you reason about classes inside modules. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Classes inside modules. Then connect it to Constant paths. The remaining syllabus points—Organizing related types—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Example: Nested Classes and Namespaces
content_blocks.code:
class Greeter
  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
  def greet
    "Hello, #{@name}!"
  end
end
puts Greeter.new("Mina").greet

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports nested classes and namespaces. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for nested classes and namespaces using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Organizing related types), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.
